name: Tamang
confidence_why: Hari, Taylor and Pike (1970), working on the Nuwakot dialect, state that word stress always falls on the first syllable, but Mazaudon (2005), the principal Tamang specialist whose own fieldwork is on Eastern Tamang, remarks in passing that Tamang syllables appear about equally stressed, and Regmi (2019) says only that stress is not distinctive, so the initial-stress reading rests on one older first-hand description that no later study confirms or directly refutes.

catalog_quote: C. Stress Some observations about word stress and intonational stress: 1. In Western Tamang the basic word stress falls always on the first syllable of a word. 2. Intonational stress on the last syllable of a word before a phrase juncture or sentence final can be quite intense and change the pattern. This varia- tion, however, is conditioned by higher level intonation factors. 3. As to word stress the tense mid-rising contour tends to be deceptive, especially on bi- and tri- syllabic morphemes or words because the first syllable is lower than the following. A tuned ear, however, hears the word stress on the first syllable inspite of the rise on the second. ... sweep_summary: Only one titled item for west2415: Pittman 1970 'Gurung, Tamang, Thakali, Sherpa, and Chepang prosodies' (Part II of the Hale & Pike SIL report, ERIC ED046002). The full Part II scan (24 MB, 136 pp.) was downloaded from archive.org and the Pittman paper read in full (the scanned text): it is a comparative register/tone paper in which Tamang 'high/mid/low stressed vs unstressed' are four lexical word-base classes matched to Gurung/Thakali tone classes; it makes no statement about which syllable carries stress, so it is silent on the catalog's classification (fixed: initial syllable), and Part I's editors state Hari's later analysis supersedes this scheme. The catalog's deciding source (Hari, Taylor & Pike 1970, Part I sec. II.C, pp. 116-117: 'the basic word stress falls always on the first syllable of a word') was re-read and confirmed verbatim; no new source supersedes it. archive.org and ERIC were reached directly by URL.

new_statements.quote: C. Stress. Some observations about word stress and intonational stress: 1. In Western Tamang the basic word stress falls always on the first syllable of a word. 2. Intonational stress on the last syllable of a word before a phrase juncture or sentence final can be quite intense and change the pattern. This variation, however, is conditioned by higher level intonation factors. 3. ... A tuned ear, however, hears the word stress on the first syllable inspite of the rise on the second. ... Word stress in Western Tamang, however, is not manifested by high pitch and falls, but by a certain intensity in the consonant and vowel onset of the stressed syllable and a slight degree of length on the closing element of the syllable.

new_statements.reading: Fixed initial word stress, weight-blind, independent of the four-way lexical tone (clear/breathy x level/falling); realized by onset intensity and slight length, not pitch. A phrase-final intonational prominence can overlay it but is explicitly attributed to higher-level intonation. This is the same passage the catalog already codes from; re-read in this search of works with stress in the title and confirmed verbatim (minor scanned errors 'matifested', 'onse' aside).

tone_statements.quote: Each monosyllabic word, in languages of the TGTM group, can carry one of four tones. The phonetic value (mainly pitch) of these tones varies from place to place ... the languages of the TGTM group do not distinguish four tones on each syllable of a word (which would make 16 melodies for a two-syllable word) but only four tones per word. ... In five dialects out of eight, Risiangku and Sahu Tamang, Tukche and Syang Thakali, and Ghachok Gurung, tone-1 and tone-2 words ‘are high with a clear voice quality; tone-3 and tone-4 are low with a breathy voice quality.

sources.quote: 'Tamang syllables appear to be all about equally stressed.' ... 'The languages of the Bodish section ... are poor in accentual contrasts. They do not generally give prominence, either by way of F0 or intensity, to one syllable per unit. Either all syllables have roughly equal prominence, as in the TGTM group, or one syllable per unit is weak.' (Her fieldwork is Risiangku = Eastern Tamang; statement is made for the Tamang/TGTM group. Same paper p.3 cites Hari, Taylor & Pike 1970:82 approvingly on the morpheme as tone domain.)
sources.note: Leading Tamang phonologist states TGTM/Tamang syllables have roughly equal prominence (no one-syllable stress) - a group-level counter-statement to fixed: initial syllable; should be cited as a caution on the record (Eastern-dialect based).

sources.quote: In the summer of 1969, Kenneth Pike, Austin Hale, and Doreen Taylor, working on Tamang with Karna Bahadur Tamang, came up with a three-tone, two-stress system with four classes ... a comparison of the many cognates which they share revealed that words which are (a) high stressed in Tamang are clear intense in Gurung and clear high level in Thakali, (b) unstressed in Tamang are clear relaxed in Gurung and clear extra-high falling in Thakali, (c) mid stressed in Tamang are breathy rising in Gurung and breathy low rising-falling in Thakali, and (d) low stressed in Tamang are breathy low in Gurung and breathy low level in Thakali
sources.locator: Pittman 1970, sec. 2 (p. 2) and sec. 3 with Table 3 (pp. 2-3); the scanned text. Same four-class scheme restated in Pittman & Glover, 'Proto-Tamang-Gurung-Thakali', same volume, pp. 9-10 (djvu lines 906-944) and p. ~12 (lines 1106-1111).
sources.note: Comparative register/tone paper (Tamang-Gurung-Thakali-Sherpa-Chepang). For Tamang it only relays the preliminary 1969 Pike/Hale/Taylor analysis: word-bases fall into four lexical classes labelled 'high stressed', 'mid stressed', 'low stressed', 'unstressed', which Pittman matches to the Gurung clear/breathy and Thakali tone classes and to his K/G (voiceless/voiced) register hypothesis; sec. 8 lists stress among the possible exponents of the register contrast alongside pitch, tenseness, fortis/lenis onset, length and breathiness. sources.note: From the Crossref abstract: the TGTM tonal split (merger of onset voicing series > split of an old two-tone system into four) is phonologically completed in all dialects studied, but traces of manner and phonation (breathiness, residual onset voicing) survive to different degrees per dialect; proposes a 'law' that breathiness used as a tone cue is retained only while the tone's pitch stays low; dialect-by-dialect pitch values and cue retention for the four tones, Western Tamang (Sahugaon) among them.
